the Vγ9 Vδ2 γδT cell population expands within 10 weeks after birth, and that this expansion occurs in a TCR-dependent manner.

the development of the immune system in humans, and in particular, the role of γδ T cells in this process.
the role that Vγ9V δ 2 T cells play in the immune system.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Vγ9VΔ2 T cells are the most abundant γδ T cell subset in human blood.
Vγ9VΔ2 T cells, which have a fetal-derived TCR, expand and acquire cytotoxic functions early after birth, likely in response to environmental phosphoantigene exposure.

the human fetal Vγ9/δ2 T cells have a public TCR repertoire, which is expanded after birth and differentiated into cytotoxic effector T cells, and that the expansion of public TCR Vγ9/Δ2 T cells is not affected by the BCG vaccine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the public fetal Vγ2Vδ2 TCR repertoire expands and differentiates into potent effector cells in the absence of microbial exposure early postpartum.

the Vγ9/δ2 T cells, which are the major human γδ T cell subset, are rapidly primed upon birth, likely upon exposure to microbial phosphoantigene, and the Vγ9 T cells are rapidly primed to become potent effector cells.
the human Vγ9/Vδ2 T cell repertoire is established during the fetal life and is further shaped by the postnatal microbial environment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the public Vγ9Vγ2 T cell population, which is present in the human fetus, expands rapidly after birth.
Vγ9Vγ2 T cells are primed by the environment early after birth, and the public T cell receptor repertoire that is shared among humans is selected for.

human Vγδ T cells, particularly the Vγ9+Vδ2+ T cells, are primed in utero and rapidly expand and differentiate in response to environmental exposure to phosphoantigen, which is generated by a variety human pathogens, including mycobacteria.
